title: Bobble stitch
subtitle: A cluster of trebles pushed out on the public side
excerpt: The bobble is five trebles worked into the same stitch, all joined together at the top and pushed outward by the surrounding flat fabric. This tutorial covers the construction, the WS/RS working position, and how to keep bobbles even.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (Internet Archive). Textured stitch patterns including bobble and cluster constructions. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), textured crochet techniques.
heroPrompt: A close-up swatch of bobble stitch in cream DK cotton, showing the round raised bobbles pushing forward from a background of flat double crochet rows. Soft natural light, plain background.

glossaryTerms.definition: Five trebles worked into the same base stitch, each left incomplete (two loops on hook after the last yarn-over step), then all closed together with a single final yarn-over. The cluster pushes outward on the public side of the fabric.

content.text: is five incomplete trebles stacked into the same stitch, joined at the top. Each treble is left with two loops remaining instead of being finished off; after five of them, there are six loops on the hook (five pairs from each treble plus the standing loop). One final yarn over pulls through all six together and the cluster pops outward.

attrs.title: The bobble sits on the wrong side unless you plan for it
attrs.body: When you work on the right side of the fabric, the bobble pops toward you. On a flat piece worked back and forth, bobble rows are usually worked from the wrong side so the bobble pushes forward onto the public face. Check the pattern: "RS facing" bobbles push toward you (away from the viewer when worn); "WS facing" bobbles push away from you (toward the viewer).

content.text: Yarn over, insert hook into the next stitch, yarn over, pull through the stitch. Three loops on hook. Yarn over, pull through two loops. Two loops remain. Stop — do NOT pull through the last two. The first incomplete treble is on the hook.

Yarn over again, insert into the SAME stitch, yarn over, pull through. Now four loops on hook. Yarn over, pull through two. Three loops remain (two from the second treble, one from the first). Stop before the final pull-through.
Repeat step 2 three more times (for a 5-treble bobble). After the fifth incomplete treble: six loops on hook.
Yarn over and pull through all six loops at once. One loop remains. The bobble is closed.
Optional: ch 1 to lock the bobble top. Some patterns include this closing chain to stop the bobble collapsing; others do not. Follow the pattern.
Row 1 (RS): ch 1, dc in each chain across (20 dc). Turn.
Row 2 (WS, bobble row): ch 3, *dc in next 3 sts, 5-tr bobble in next st; repeat from * across, dc in last st (5 bobbles). Turn.
Row 3 (RS): ch 1, dc in each stitch across (20 dc). Turn.
Row 4 (WS): ch 3, dc in next st, *5-tr bobble in next st, dc in next 3 sts; repeat from * to last 2 sts, bobble in next st, dc in last st. Turn.
Repeat rows 1-4 for the bobble stitch pattern.

attrs.heading: Bobble problems
attrs.intro: Three problems that come up with bobble stitch.

items.symptom: The bobble does not stand out from the fabric
items.cause: Working on the right side so the bobble pops toward you rather than toward the viewer.
items.fix: Work bobble rows from the wrong side of the fabric. The bobble then pushes toward the public face.

items.symptom: The top of the bobble looks messy or has a visible loop
items.cause: The final pull-through was not drawn tight enough, or the optional locking chain was omitted where needed.
items.fix: Draw the final pull-through firmly to close the bobble top. If the bobble head still shows a loop, work a ch 1 lock stitch immediately after.

items.symptom: The stitch count shifts after a bobble row
items.cause: The bobble top is being treated as a separate stitch by counting the closing chain or the top of the bobble separately.
items.fix: The bobble counts as one stitch. Work the next dc into the stitch after the bobble's base stitch, not into the bobble top itself.

content.text: The popcorn is the natural comparison: it uses five complete trebles into the same stitch (finished off individually rather than stacked), then removes the hook and re-inserts it into the first treble of the group to close it. The popcorn stands taller and more defined than the bobble; the bobble is softer. Try both in the same swatch to see the difference.
